title: Undyed Silk, Uncarved Wood

zh.text: 絕聖棄智，民利百倍；絕仁棄義，民復孝慈；絕巧棄利，盜賊無有。此三者以為文不足，故令有所屬﹕見素抱樸，少私寡欲。

gloss.0: to cut, as a silk thread is cut
gloss.1: sage; here the title and ideal of sagehood
gloss.6: gain: here good, the people’s gain
gloss.23: profit: here a thing to throw away (the same graph)
gloss.40: to cause, to let; to order
gloss.43: zhǔ: to fasten to, to belong to
gloss.45: xiàn: to show (or jiàn: to see)

rendering: Cut off [[humaneness, throw away right conduct|renyi]]:
the people go back to devotion and tender care.
These three, as [[ornament|wen]], are not enough.
So let there be [[something to fasten to|zhu]]:
[[less of what is private, fewer wants|shao]].

jue.title: 絕: a knife on the thread
jue.body: The first word of the passage, used three times, is a weaver’s word. The Shuowen defines 絕 as 斷絲也, “to cut silk thread”, and reads the graph as 糸, silk, with 刀, a knife, and 卩. To 絕 is to sever a line that was continuous: a thread, a road, a family with no heir, a friendship. It is sudden and final; a cut thread is not “reduced”. Passage 14 ended with a thread to follow, the lead thread of Dao; this passage begins with threads to cut. The partner verb, 棄, is [[as hard|qi]]. English “renounce”, “give up”, or “abandon” are words of the will and the conscience. The Chinese verbs are acts of the hand. Note also what is cut. In each pair it is the thing that the schools of the age praised most.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 糸部: 絕，斷絲也。从糸从刀从卩。

qi.title: 棄: the abandoned child
qi.body: 棄 is one of the darkest pictures in the script. The Shuowen defines it 捐也, “to cast off”, and takes it apart: two hands at the bottom push a winnowing basket, and at the top is 𠫓, which it explains as 逆子也, “a child head-down”: a new-born. The graph shows an infant carried out in a basket to be exposed. This was done. The founder of the Zhou people, Lord Millet, was named 棄, “the Abandoned”: his mother left him three times, in a lane, in a wood, and on ice, and oxen, woodcutters, and birds kept him alive. So the word that the passage uses for cleverness, right conduct, and profit is the word for the hardest thing a parent can do. The line just after it speaks of 孝慈, the care between parent and child. Was that placed there by chance?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 𠦒部: 棄，捐也。从廾推𠦒棄之，从𠫓。𠫓，逆子也。

sheng.title: The book cuts off its own hero
sheng.body: 聖 is the 聖人, the sage, who is the model in more than twenty passages of this book. Here the text says: cut it off. Readers have felt the shock for two thousand years. One answer: what is cut is the title and the cult, the “sage-kings” whom Confucians and Mohists held up to rulers as a standard. The Shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “to pass through, to understand through”, and puts it under 耳, the ear: at root it is a way of hearing, and a way of hearing cannot be an office. Wang Bi takes the plainest line: 聖智，才之善也, “sagehood and cleverness are the best of talents”, and still the text cuts them. The other answer is that this line is [[not the oldest form of the passage|guodian]]. A later follower [[took the line as far as it would go|quqie]]. Would the sage of the other passages mind?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 耳部: 聖，通也。从耳呈聲。

guodian.title: The oldest copy does not attack the sage
guodian.body: In 1993 bamboo slips with parts of the Laozi were found in a tomb at Guodian, closed about 300 BCE. Their text of this passage is reported to differ in two of the three pairs, and in the order. First: 絕智棄辯, “cut off cleverness, throw away debate”, and the people gain a hundredfold. Second: “cut off skill, throw away profit”, as in our third pair. Third, in place of “cut off humaneness, throw away right conduct”: two graphs that scholars read as 絕偽棄詐 or 絕偽棄慮, “cut off artifice, throw away deceit (or scheming)”, and the people go back to family feeling. In that version nothing is said against 聖, 仁, or 義. The targets are the debaters and the schemers, whom Confucians disliked too. If the reading is right, the attack on Confucian virtue was written in later. Both Mawangdui silk texts, copied about 200 BCE, already have it: silk text B reads 絕聖棄知 and 絕仁棄義. We render the received text. It has a quieter ancestor.

li.title: 利 twice: gain for the people, profit to discard
li.body: The same character stands in line 2 and in line 5, with opposite signs. 民利百倍: the people’s 利 is a hundred times greater. 絕巧棄利: throw 利 away. English hides the clash with two words, “benefit” and “profit”. In Chinese it is plain to see, and it is the point. 利 is the sharp edge of a blade and the yield of a harvest: advantage. The Mohists made 利, the benefit of all, the test of each policy; the Legalists built the state on the fact that each person runs after 利. The passage separates what the schools ran together. When each one chases advantage, the sum is loss. When the chase is dropped, the people are better off, and the text measures the result with a trader’s figure: a hundredfold. Passage 11 has the same word in its last couplet, set against 用, use.

renyi.title: The cure for the last passage’s illness
renyi.body: This line answers passage 18, which said: when the great road falls to ruin, there are 仁 and 義; when the six kin are out of tune, there are 孝 and 慈. Now the text proposes to cut the first pair, and promises that the people will 復, go back to, the second. So the book does not want less family feeling. It claims that devotion and tender care are there before the teaching, and that the teaching covers them. A child loves its parents before it knows the word 孝. Add a public standard, with praise for those who meet it and shame for those who fail, and the same child begins to perform. Mencius, the great defender of 仁義, would agree with half of this: he also held that the feeling comes first, and gave the case of anyone who sees a small child about to fall into a well. The two differ on what naming does to the feeling.

qiao.title: 巧 and 利: the workshop and the market
qiao.body: 巧 is a craftsman’s skill; the Shuowen says 技也, “technique”, and the graph has 工, the carpenter’s square. With 利, profit, it names the two new forces of the age. Iron tools and coined money spread through the states after about 500 BCE. Cities grew, and with them workshops for lacquer, bronze inlay, and silk, and merchants who became richer than lords; one of them, Lü Buwei, made himself chief minister of Qin. Fine goods were the visible sign of the change, and the Laozi speaks of them in other places: “goods hard to come by make a person’s conduct go wrong” (12). The link to robbers is practical. Passage 3 says: do not prize rare goods, and the people will not steal. A thing that is made to be envied has, in a sense, already made its thief.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 工部: 巧，技也。从工丂聲。

daozei.title: 盜: one who drools over a dish
daozei.body: The Shuowen’s entry for 盜 is almost a joke. The definition is 私利物也, “to take a thing for private gain”. Then the parts: the lower half is 皿, a dish. The upper half is an old graph for spittle, written with water and an open mouth; and the dictionary says 㳄欲皿者, “one who drools with desire for the dish”. A robber, in this graph, is first a person who looks at someone else’s bowl with a wet mouth. 賊 is the harder word; it has 戈, a dagger-axe, in it, and means one who does armed harm: a bandit, a rebel, an assassin. So 盜賊 covers the range from want to violence. Note where the Shuowen puts the origin: in 欲, wanting, the last word of this passage. The cure at the end, 寡欲, [[fewer wants|shao]], is aimed at the mouth above the dish.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 㳄部: 盜，私利物也。从㳄，㳄欲皿者。
Shuowen Jiezi, 戈部: 賊，敗也。从戈則聲。

quqie.title: “Steal a hook, and die; steal a state, and be a lord”
quqie.body: A chapter of the Zhuangzi called “Rifling Trunks” quotes this passage and turns it into the fiercest political essay of early China. You tie your trunk with strong cords against thieves, it says; then a great thief comes, lifts the whole trunk, and is only afraid that the cords may break. Sagely laws are those cords. Its example was recent history. In 481 BCE the Tian family murdered the lord of Qi and took the state, and with it all the rites, measures, and moral teaching that the sages had made for Qi, which then protected the thieves. 竊鉤者誅，竊國者為諸侯: “one who steals a belt-hook is put to death; one who steals a state becomes a feudal lord”. And at a lord’s gate, it adds, there is always 仁義. Its conclusion borrows our first line: 絕聖棄知，大盜乃止, “cut off sagehood, throw away cleverness, and the great robbers will stop”.

wen.title: 文: pattern, ornament, text, culture
wen.body: 此三者以為文不足 is a hard clause, and all turns on 文. The Shuowen defines 文 as 錯畫也, “crossed lines”: a pattern, as in woven cloth or a tattoo. From pattern come ornament, a written character, a text, and “culture” itself; Confucius called the heritage of Zhou 斯文, “this culture”. At least three readings stand. One: “these three statements, as wording, are not enough”; the three bans are too bare. Wang Bi reads it so. Two: “these three [sagehood, humaneness, skill] are mere ornament, and do not suffice” to govern. Three: “these three, held as doctrine, fall short”. Our “as ornament” keeps the ambiguity between one and two. In each reading the next step is the same: the passage sees that to cut is not enough, and offers something to hold. It is a thread image once more: after the knife of [[絕|jue]], the pattern of 文, and then [[plain silk|su]].
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 文部: 文，錯畫也。象交文。

zhu.title: Wang Bi: a ban needs a home
zhu.body: 故令有所屬: “so cause there to be a place to belong”. 屬 (zhǔ here) is to join on, to attach; the Shuowen says 連也, “to connect”, and oddly files it under 尾, the tail: what follows on behind a body. Wang Bi explains why the turn is needed. He grants that the three things cut off are goods: 聖智，才之善也。仁義，人之善也。巧利，用之善也。 “Sagehood and cleverness are the best of talent. Humaneness and right conduct are the best of persons. Skill and profit are the best of utility.” 而直云絕，文甚不足，不令之有所屬，無以見其指. “But to say only ‘cut off’ is very insufficient as a statement; unless they are given something to attach to, there is no way to show what is pointed at.” A person told only what to drop has empty hands, and empty hands pick up the next thing. So the passage ends with four positive acts. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to say 此三言也, “these three sayings”, which supports his reading.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 尾部: 屬，連也。从尾蜀聲。

su.title: 素: silk before the dye
su.body: The Shuowen defines 素 as 白緻繒也: “white, close-woven silk”. It is cloth as it comes from the loom, before any colour, and so “plain”, “basic”, “what a thing is to begin with”; today it is the word for a chemical element and for a diet with no meat. The age thought with this image. Mozi, it is told, saw silk being dyed and sighed: put it in blue and it is blue, put it in yellow and it is yellow; one must be careful what one is dipped in. Confucius, asked about a line of verse, said 繪事後素, “the painting comes after the plain ground”, and his student saw that rites, too, come second. So the schools agreed that there is a ground. The Laozi says: show it. The verb 見 has two readings. As xiàn it is “to show, to let be seen”; as jiàn it is “to look at”. We chose “show”. The other is “keep the plain in sight”.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 素部: 素，白緻繒也。从糸、𠂹，取其澤也。

pu.title: 抱樸: the phrase that became a man’s name
pu.body: 樸 is wood before the knife; the Shuowen glosses it 木素也, “the 素 of wood”, so the dictionary itself ties the two images of this line together: silk before dye, wood before carving. The verb is 抱, to hold in the arms against the chest, as one carries a child or a bundle. It is a verb of the whole body. Passage 10 and passage 22 use it for 抱一, “to hold the One”. Six hundred years later, about 320 CE, a scholar from the south named Ge Hong took this phrase for his name and for the title of his book: 抱朴子, “the Master who Holds the Uncarved Wood”. The book is a main source for Chinese alchemy and the search for long life, with recipes for elixirs of cinnabar and gold. The plain block had by then become the emblem of a learned and complex religion. What are your arms around, most of the day?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 木部: 樸，木素也。从木菐聲。

shao.title: Less and fewer, not none
shao.body: 少私寡欲: “make the private small, make wants few”. After three total verbs, cut and throw away, the positive programme is modest. It does not say 無私, no self-interest, or 無欲, no desire, though both phrases exist in this book (7, 1). It says 少 and 寡: less, fewer. English versions with “selflessness” or the ascetic “eschew lusts” of Legge’s verse make it a harder and more Christian demand than it is. 私 is what is one’s own, as against 公, the common. The Shuowen says it was at first a word for grain, and the right-hand part, 厶, is the old graph for “private”, which Han Fei explained as a line that curls around itself. 欲 is appetite; see [[the drooling mouth|daozei]]. The measure is practical: a household can have its own share and its wants, in a size that needs no robbers to supply it and attracts none.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 禾部: 私，禾也。从禾厶聲。北道名禾主人曰私主人。

xue.title: Where does the passage end?
xue.body: The next passage begins with four characters, 絕學無憂: “cut off learning: no worry”. Many scholars think they belong here, as the last line of this passage. The verb is the 絕 that opens each of the three pairs above. The form fits: 少私寡欲 and 絕學無憂 are two lines of four. And the Mawangdui silk texts, which have no chapter breaks, are reported to run straight on from one to the other. The oldest evidence points the other way. On the Guodian slips this passage is reported to stand in one bundle and to end at 少私寡欲, and 絕學亡憂 opens the text of passage 20 in another bundle. So about 300 BCE the line already belonged with what follows. If a later reader hears it here too, the list of things to cut grows to seven, and ends with the one that a reader of books least expects. You are, at this moment, in the act of 學.

legge.title: Legge breaks into verse
legge.body: In the first half Legge adds a subject and a mood: “If we could renounce our sageness”. The Chinese has no “if”, no “we”, and no “our”; it gives an order, or states a law. With “we… our” he makes it a confession by the ruling class, which is a fair reading, and with “if we could” a sigh, which is his own. Then, at the hard clause on 文, he does something unusual: he changes to rhymed verse, four lines that end “eschew”. He read the close of the passage as a rhymed saying, and tried to show it. The cost is high. 素 and 樸, the silk and the wood, become “simple views, and courses plain and true”, and the two craft images vanish. 欲 becomes “lusts”, a word from the English Bible. Compare the Chinese: eight characters, two things held in the hands, two things made smaller.
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

practice.title: One thing with no finish on it
practice.body: Find one thing today that is 素 or 樸: a thing with no finish on it. A board with no paint. A bowl of plain rice. A wall with nothing on it. Tap water. A sentence with no adjective. Give it one full minute of attention, and note the small restlessness that asks for more: colour, salt, a picture, a clever phrase. That restlessness is 欲 in its mildest form. Do not fight it. Then try the two verbs on yourself, in the passage’s own modest measure. [[少私|shao]]: once today, when you would say “my”, see if the sentence works without it. 寡欲: when you next want to buy or add something, wait one day. The passage does not ask for a monk. It asks for less, and promises that less will not feel like loss once the hands are [[around something plain|pu]].

lenses.ground: Three hammer blows, and then a quiet close. Each blow has the same form: [[cut off|jue]] X, [[throw away|qi]] Y, and a result for the people. Cut [[sagehood|sheng]] and cleverness: the people [[gain|li]] a hundredfold. Cut [[humaneness and right conduct|renyi]]: they go back to family feeling. Cut [[skill|qiao]] and profit: [[no robbers|daozei]]. Then the text comments on itself, which it seldom does: these three, [[as ornament or as wording|wen]], are not enough, so here is [[something to belong to|zhu]]. The something is two images and two measures: [[undyed silk|su]], [[uncarved wood|pu]], [[less that is private, fewer wants|shao]]. The pictures are all from the workshop: a knife on a thread, a child in a basket, a pattern in cloth, white silk, a log. [[The oldest copy|guodian]] is reported to aim the first blows at other targets, and the passage may have [[one more line|xue]].
lenses.inner: Read the six things to be cut as six ways in which a person builds a self to show. I am wise; I am sharp. I am kind; I do my duty. I am skilled; I do well. Each is good, as [[Wang Bi|zhu]] admits, and each is a dye. The passage does not ask what you should be in place of these. It asks what the cloth was before it went into the vat. [[素|su]] and [[樸|pu]] are not achievements, and you cannot acquire them; they are what is there when the acquiring stops. So the practice has two motions, as the passage does. First the cut, which is quick. Then something for the arms to hold, since a mind that has only dropped things will pick up the next shiny one. The close is kind: [[less|shao]], not none. Who are you before you are good at anything?
lenses.leading: A ruler of the time heard advice from three sides. Confucians: be a sage, teach humaneness and duty. Strategists and debaters: be clever. Economic advisers: promote crafts and trade. The passage cuts all three, and its test is one thing only, three times: what happens to 民, the people. That is the part to keep. A programme is judged by what it does to those below, and not by how wise, good, or skilled it makes those above look. The [[Zhuangzi’s essay|quqie]] adds the cynical corollary: moral language is the first thing that a usurper steals. In an organisation, look for the three dyes: the cult of the brilliant founder, the values on the wall, the bonus scheme that makes people [[look at each other’s bowls|daozei]]. The passage also knows that [[a ban alone leaves a hole|zhu]]. What plain thing would your people hold if the slogans went?
lenses.nature: No river is wise and no forest is virtuous. Plain things in nature are not poor: a block of oak has every bowl and beam in it, and white silk can take any colour. Carving and dyeing are choices that cannot be reversed. For this reason the craft images are exact where “simplicity” is vague. A [[樸|pu]] is not a small or humble thing; it is a thing with its possibilities intact. Ecology has the same thought. A meadow that nobody has “improved” holds more kinds of life than a lawn. An old tree that foresters call over-mature is a city for birds and insects. To [[show the plain|su]] in a landscape is to leave some of it with no finish. Where near you is there ground that has not been dyed?
lenses.practice: Take [[one plain thing|practice]] today and stay with it for a minute. Then choose one of the three pairs for a week. Cleverness: in one meeting or talk, do not make the smart remark. Virtue: do one kind act that nobody can find out about. Skill and profit: do one thing that you are good at, slowly and badly, as a beginner, for no result. Each time, see what is under the thing that you put down. It may be only awkwardness at first. The passage says that under it is something to hold with both arms. If the first line still troubles you, read [[how the oldest copy puts it|guodian]] and [[why the book would cut its own hero|sheng]]. And see what happened when [[a Victorian tried to rhyme the ending|legge]].

plates.title: Silk as it leaves the loom
plates.lesson: Look at the bottom first: 糸, the silk sign, a skein with two twists and loose ends. You have seen it on the left side of [[絕|jue]], where a knife is beside it. Here it stands at the foot, full size. The top of the character has three level strokes and a vertical. The Shuowen explains it as 𠂹, an old graph for a thing that hangs down, and says 取其澤也, “it is chosen for the sheen”: fine raw silk that hangs in smooth, glossy folds. The definition is plain: 白緻繒也, white, close-woven silk. Now see how far a word can go from a bolt of cloth. Undyed, so “white”: mourning clothes were of 素. Not coloured, so “plain”: 樸素 is “simple and unadorned”, a pair made of the two images of this passage. Not yet worked, so “the base material”: 元素 is a chemical element, 因素 a factor, 要素 an essential. With no meat or strong flavour: 素食, the food of Buddhist monks. As usual: 素來, “all along, in the ordinary way”. Old texts speak of a “plain king”, 素王, a person who has the worth of a ruler and no throne; later ages gave that title to Confucius. One more cousin: 索, a rope, looks alike and is also made of 糸. The passage sets 素 against [[文|wen]], pattern. Before a pattern there must be cloth.
plates.brush: Ten strokes: four above, six below. A level stroke; a second level stroke; a vertical through both; then the third level stroke, the longest, on which the top rests. Keep the three level lines apart by even gaps; the vertical does not go below the third. Then the silk. Two strokes of one kind, each down to the left and then back to the right: the two twists, the lower one wider. A dot closes the second twist. Now watch the last three strokes, which are different from the silk sign when it stands at the left: a vertical in the centre that ends in a small hook, then a dot to the left of it, and a dot to the right. They are the loose ends of the skein, and they stand like three small feet. The whole character is tall and narrow in the waist, with the widest line just above the middle.

plates.title: Two hands, a basket, a child
plates.lesson: Read this character from the top down, as the Shuowen does. The top four strokes are 𠫓. It is 子, a child, written upside down; the Shuowen says 逆子也, “a child reversed”, and the same form is in 育, to give birth and to rear, and in 流, to flow, where it is commonly explained as a child that comes out with the waters. Under the child is a shape with crossed lines, which the Shuowen reads as a winnowing basket with a handle, the kind used to toss grain and to carry out rubbish. At the bottom, in the old forms, are two hands, 廾; the regular script has changed them and the basket’s foot into a shape that looks like 木, a tree. Oracle-bone forms of the graph are commonly described in the same way: two hands, a basket, a child with drops around it. So the whole is: to carry a new-born out in a basket. The meaning is “to discard”, and it has not softened: 放棄 is to give up, 拋棄 to forsake, 棄權 to waive a right. The short form 弃, with only the child and the two hands, is very old; the Shuowen records it as the ancient-script form, and it is the mainland standard today. The founder of the Zhou people [[had this word for his name|qi]]. The passage uses it for cleverness, right conduct, and profit: things, it suggests, that their parents will find hard to leave.
plates.brush: Twelve strokes, in three levels. The child first: a dot; a level stroke; then a stroke that goes down to the left and turns back to the right; and a last dot. Then the basket: a long level stroke, the widest line in the character; two short verticals that start above it and cut down through it; and a short level stroke that joins them. Then the lower part: a level stroke; a long vertical, drawn downward from above the basket through all the level strokes to the foot; and the last two strokes, one that falls to the left and one that presses out to the right. Watch that final pair. They spread wide, like arms that hold the load away from the body. The danger in this character is weight at the top. A good hand keeps the child light and lets the two long level lines and the final pair carry the whole.

plates.title: A wet mouth over a dish
plates.lesson: Three parts, and the Shuowen reads them as a little scene. At the upper left are three drops, 氵, water. Beside them is 欠. This is a person with the mouth wide open: it means to yawn, to breathe out, to lack, and it is the right side of 欲, desire, and of 歌 (to sing), 吹 (to blow), 飲 (to drink). Water and an open mouth together are 㳄, the old graph for spittle, the word now written 涎. Under both is 皿, a dish. You know it from 盈, [[full|shao]], and 盤 (a tray), 盆 (a basin), 盡 (used up; commonly explained as a hand that scrubs an empty dish). So: one who drools over a dish. The Shuowen says exactly this, 㳄欲皿者, and defines the word as 私利物也, to make a thing one’s private gain. In classical Chinese 盜 is the robber and 賊 the one who does violence; in the modern language they have nearly changed places, and 盜 is the thief. It is a good graph for the passage’s argument about [[where robbers come from|daozei]]. The dish is someone else’s. The crime in the picture has not yet happened; there is only the mouth, and the water in it. The mainland short form, 盗, writes 次 on top: the spittle has lost a drop.
plates.brush: Twelve strokes: three, four, five. The water: a dot, a second dot, and a stroke that flicks up to the right. Then 欠: a short stroke that falls to the left; a level stroke that ends in a hook; then the person below, a long stroke that falls to the left and one that presses out to the right. These two must be kept short and flat, because they have a dish under them. Then 皿: left side; a stroke for the top and right side; two short verticals inside; and the long base line. Watch the twelfth stroke. It is the widest line in the character, and it runs out past both sides of the dish like a table. All that is above leans over it. In a well-written 盜 the upper half is a little too large and a little too far forward for comfort. That is right for this word.
